query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the Cu content in the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating enhances the in situ formation of a protective Cu-oxide nanolayer during high-temperature sliding (~500°C), which in turn reduces wear rate and alters the microscopic deformation behavior compared to the baseline alloy composition.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating deposited on a conventional metal substrate with baseline Cu content.
generation.intervention: Increase the Cu content in the alloy composition relative to the baseline condition.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding tests around 500°C using a pin‐on‐disk apparatus under controlled mechanical load and sliding speed.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced formation of a continuous, nanostructured Cu-oxide layer on the coating surface during sliding.
generation.mechanism: The elevated Cu content promotes rapid oxidation at high temperature, generating a protective Cu-oxide layer that decreases direct metal-to-metal contact, mitigates plastic deformation, and lowers wear rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Cu-enhanced coating will exhibit a lower wear rate and show modified microscopic deformation patterns (such as reduced debris formation and more stable surface features) relative to the baseline coating.
generation.baseline: The coating with the standard Cu content in the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy.
generation.boundary: This prediction is expected to hold under high-temperature sliding conditions (~500°C), at controlled load and sliding speed settings typical of pin‐on‐disk tests.
generation.uncertainty: While there is supporting evidence for protective oxide formation at high temperatures, the exact quantitative impact on wear rate and the details of the microscopic deformation mechanisms remain to be fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy coatings on conventional metal substrates: one with standard Cu content (baseline) and one with increased Cu content. Subject both sets to pin‐on‐disk sliding tests at ~500°C under identical loads and sliding speeds. Use in situ microscopy and post-test surface analyses (SEM, XPS, EDS) to examine the formation of surface oxide layers and assess wear rates and microscopic deformation features.
measurements: Chemical composition and identification of oxides on the worn surface (XPS/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the increased Cu content coating does not show a statistically significant reduction in wear rate, fails to develop a continuous Cu-oxide layer relative to the baseline, or if the microscopic deformation patterns remain indistinguishable from the baseline, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractCompared with traditional alloys, high-entropy alloys have better mechanical properties and corrosion resistance. However, their mechanical properties and microstructural evolution behavior are unclear due to their complex composition. Machine learning has powerful data processing and analysis capabilities, that provides technical advantages for in-depth study of the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys. Thus, we combined machine learning and molecular dynamics to predict the mechanical properties of FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloys. The optimal multiple linear regression machine learning algorithm predicts that the optimal composition is Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13 high-entropy alloy, with a tensile strength of 28.25 GPa. Furthermore, molecular dynamics is used to verify the predicted mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys, and it is found that the error between the tensile strength predicted by machine learning and the tensile strength obtained by molecular dynamics simulation is within 0.5%. Moreover, the tensile-compression asymmetry of Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13 high-entropy alloy increased with the increase of temperature and Cu content and the decrease of Fe content.

For NiX, its worn track dimensions also increase at 400 °C compared to those at RT, but the worn surface remains relatively smooth and is free of debris and micro-pits (Fig. S7b). This uncovers that NiX still outperforms Ni3X in resisting the elastic–plastic deformation involved with abrasive wear even at 400 °C. The higher high-temperature hardness of NiX may be responsible for the low wear rate compared to Ni3X at 400 °C (Fig. 3A). Nanoindentation tests (Fig. S2) also show that H on the worn surface of NiX (5.9 GPa) at 400 °C is higher than that of Ni3X (4.9 GPa). Deposition of high entropy alloy FeCoNiMnCu on SS-304 was carried out by microwave energy for application in “solid oxide fuel-cell (SOFC) interconnects”. The ball-milling has been performed by taking “Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, and Cu” in equal 20 wt. % of before deposited on SS-304 substrate. The deposited steel with 20% Fe 20% Co 20% Ni 20% Mn 20% Cu high entropy alloy (HEA) was exposed to thermal-exposure in the air for up to 10 weeks at 800 °C. The uniform cladding distribution of 20% Fe 20% Co 20% Ni 20% Mn 20% Cu HEA particles can be apparently observed on SS-304 substrate by utilizing Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM), and Optical microscopy analysis. Homogeneity in the interfacial layer was evident by employing Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) characterization. Results have indicated that after the thermal exposure of deposited steel with 20% Fe 20% Co 20% Ni 20% Mn 20% Cu in the air for up to ten weeks at 800 °C, a “protective Cr2O3 layer”, and “high-entropy spinel coating” of (Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, Cu)3O4 have been formed.
